Anniversary days

Source: R/datey.R
anniversary_days.Rd

The position of a date relative to the start of its calendar year depends on whether that calendar year is a leap year or not. This means that in datey (and reality!) the start of 2020-04-01 plus 1 year is not equal to the start of 2021-04-01.

This is by design and is usually precisely what's required. But this behaviour can be awkward when anniversaries are the focus and, fictitious as it may be, the position of a date in a year is required to be the same regardless of whether the year is or is not a leap year.

To help with such cases, datey also provides anniversary days, which assume every year has 366 days but that 29 February is just under a quarter of the length of the other days. This convenient fiction ensures that anniversaries always occur at the same point in the year.

These functions are intended for special cases, e.g. when anniversaries are used to define datasets. For standard calculations, the normal approach is recommended.

Usage

start_anniversary_day_to_ymd(x)

start_anniversary_day(year, month, day, strict = TRUE)

is_start_anniversary_day(x)

Arguments

x

The datey to test or deconstruct.

year, month, day

The year (1000 to 3000), month (1 to 12) and day (1 to 31).

Note that 29 February is valid for all years.

strict

How non-compliant non-NA inputs should be handled. If strict is TRUE – the default – then execution is stopped. If strict is FALSE then NA is returned.

Value

start_anniversary_day() returns a datey the same length as its arguments.

is_start_anniversary_day() returns a logical the same length as its argument.

start_anniversary_day_to_ymd() returns a list of integer vector year, integer vector month, and integer vector day, all with the same length.

If the datey is not the start of an anniversary day then all components are NA.

See also

datey, datey_components, is_xxx_day

Examples

# Adding whole years to the start of a day can leave the day boundary,
# because days in a leap year are shorter:
t <- start_day(2020, 4, 1) + durationy(0:4)
t
#> [1] 2020-04-01.0    2021-04-01.7514 2022-04-01.7514 2023-04-01.7514
#> [5] 2024-04-01.0   
is_start_day(t)
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE

# Anniversary days stay on the anniversary:
anniversary <- start_anniversary_day(2020, 4, 1) + durationy(0:4)
is_start_anniversary_day(anniversary)
#> [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE
as.data.frame(start_anniversary_day_to_ymd(anniversary))
#>   year month day
#> 1 2020     4   1
#> 2 2021     4   1
#> 3 2022     4   1
#> 4 2023     4   1
#> 5 2024     4   1

# 29 February is an anniversary day in every year:
leap_day <- start_anniversary_day(2020, 2, 29) + durationy(0:4)
as.data.frame(start_anniversary_day_to_ymd(leap_day))
#>   year month day
#> 1 2020     2  29
#> 2 2021     2  29
#> 3 2022     2  29
#> 4 2023     2  29
#> 5 2024     2  29

# The cost is that anniversary days rarely match calendar days. Indeed, in
# 2020, a leap year, the 1 April anniversary day starts on 31 March:
anniversary[1:2]
#> [1] 2020-03-31.4349 2021-04-01.1878

# Anniversary day deconstruction is NA for non-anniversary days:
as.data.frame(start_anniversary_day_to_ymd(start_day(2020, 4, 1)))
#>   year month day
#> 1   NA    NA  NA
